questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The State and the Government' refers to.
questions.a: The state is the permanent political community with its territory, people and institutions; the government is only its temporary crew, elected or appointed for a time to run the state's affairs.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The State and the Government'.
questions.a: Governments come and go, the state remains: criticising a party is not attacking the country.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'The State and the Government', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: state = people + territory + institutions; government = the team in office

concepts.title: The State's Rulebook: An RWA Example

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The State's Rulebook: An RWA Example' refers to.
questions.a: The chapter uses a Resident Welfare Association: its rulebook decides how the committee is elected, how funds are spent and how disputes are heard; a constitution plays the same role for the state.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The State's Rulebook: An RWA Example'.
questions.a: Small societies need written rules; a huge state cannot function without one supreme rulebook.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The State's Rulebook: An RWA Example' taught, and from which source text?
Using the method 'Levels of Government', work with: local = 500, state = 200, union = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of levels.
Take the relation taught for 'Levels of Government' and work with: local = 4, state = 60, union = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of levels.
Explain in your own words what 'Levels of Government' refers to.
questions.a: India's government works at three levels, the Union at the centre, states, and local bodies in villages and cities; each level has its own powers and all play different, complementary roles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Levels of Government'.
questions.a: A subcontinent-sized democracy divides its work: big questions to the centre, local drains to the local body.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Levels of Government', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Your Part in the State' refers to.
questions.a: The state is not someone else: every citizen pays taxes, follows just laws, votes, questions wrongs and can serve; Socrates' warning that shirking rule leaves you ruled by worse men calls citizens to participate.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Your Part in the State'.
questions.a: Democracy hands the state to its citizens: stepping back is also a choice, with its own price.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Your Part in the State' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Citizens and the state (source: gees206.txt, Citizens and the state)
